source_title: Insurance Expert Jack Sughrue Explains Umbrella Insurance and Extra Liability Coverage in HelloNation
source_excerpt:
The article explains how umbrella coverage can provide added protection when certain liability claims exceed the limits of primary insurance policies.
DENVER , Oct. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What happens when a liability claim costs more than an auto or homeowners insurance policy will cover? A HelloNation article featuring insights from Insurance Expert Jack Sughrue explains when umbrella insurance and extra liability coverage may provide an added layer of protection.
The article explains that auto and homeowners insurance generally include liability protection, but every policy has limits. A serious accident or injury can create costs that exceed those limits. Umbrella insurance works with existing coverage and may help pay some remaining costs when a covered claim goes beyond the primary policy's limit.
An umbrella insurance policy does not replace auto or homeowners insurance. Instead, the main policy generally responds first. The article uses a serious car accident as an example, noting that injuries to several people could produce medical bills and other expenses beyond the available auto liability protection.
Similar situations can occur at home. If a guest is injured on a property and the homeowner is found responsible, homeowners insurance may help with the covered claim. An umbrella insurance policy may provide additional protection when the costs exceed the home policy's liability limit.
The article also identifies personal assets as an important reason to evaluate extra liability coverage. Savings, investments, and property accumulated over time may face greater financial exposure if a large judgment exceeds available insurance coverage. Reviewing personal assets alongside existing policy limits can help reveal possible gaps in protection.
Liability exposure is another consideration. The article describes liability exposure as situations that could increase the chance of being held responsible for an injury or property damage. A household's homes, vehicles, hobbies, and other activities can all affect the amount of potential risk.
Teen drivers are one example highlighted in the article. New drivers have less experience, and a serious accident can result in a costly claim. Families with teen drivers may want to review their existing auto liability limits and determine whether extra liability coverage fits their circumstances.
Features around the home can create additional liability exposure as well. A swimming pool can increase risk if a guest is injured, while frequent visitors may create more opportunities for accidents. Rental property owners may also face liability claims if someone is injured at a property they own.
The article also clarifies that umbrella insurance does not cover every loss. It generally does not pay to repair the policyholder's own vehicle or replace belongings damaged inside the home. Intentional acts and certain business claims may also be excluded, depending on the terms of the policy.
Insurance requirements can affect whether an umbrella insurance policy is available. The article notes that an insurer may require specific liability limits on underlying auto and homeowners insurance before offering umbrella coverage. These requirements ensure that the primary policies provide the first level of liability protection.
Cost is another part of the decision. The amount of coverage selected and the risks within a household can influence pricing. The number of homes, vehicles, and drivers may matter, and teen drivers or other additional risks may also affect the cost.
The article concludes that umbrella insurance may be worth considering when a household wants more protection against certain large liability claims. Examining personal assets, current insurance limits, and liability exposure can help identify potential gaps and clarify whether additional coverage fits a household's needs.
